extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of rhetoric; readers studying classical oratory (aspiring orators, lawyers, and scholars of Cicero)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging or producing effective public oratory (style, delivery, reasoning, legal learning, and character), as illustrated by Roman and Greek speakers. Useful for assessing an orator's rhetorical skills and aptitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and consistency of composition
rubrics_metrics.description: The flow of the periods, and the turn of the language, are perfectly similar throughout the whole of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A speech should read and sound as a single coherent work; too many hands or disparate styles will show. The text uses this consistency as a test for single authorship and as a mark of excellence (anti-pattern: a patchy or inconsistent style that betrays mixed composition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity and correctness of language (elocution)
rubrics_metrics.description: A purity of style and speaking the native tongue correctly is a commendable quality; 'it is not so meritorious to speak our native tongue correctly, as it is scandalous to speak it otherwise.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correctness and purity of diction are essential; while brilliance is less important than correctness, neglecting the native language is a grave fault. Example: Q. Catulus praised for 'an unblemished purity and correctness of style.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of words — weight over brilliance
rubrics_metrics.description: In the choice of his words (in which he had more regard to their weight than their brilliance)...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer words that carry appropriate force and gravity rather than merely showy vocabulary. Good diction should serve the argument, not distract from it. Anti-pattern: prioritizing flashy words at the expense of clarity or appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures and ornaments (use of rhetorical figures)
rubrics_metrics.description: The figures ... are the principal ornaments of an able speaker ... those which contribute not so much to paint and embellish our language, as to give a lustre to our sentiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures of speech should illuminate and strengthen sentiment and reasoning rather than merely ornament. Well-managed figures (Antonius had a great command of them) increase persuasive power. Overuse or irrelevant ornamentation is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of reasoning and arrangement of arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Antonius discovered every thing which could be of service to his cause, and that in the very order in which it would be most so ... like a skilful General posts the cavalry, the infantry, and the light troops, where each of them can act to most advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments must be organized strategically and presented in an order that maximizes their effect. Clarity of method and structure is critical (example: Antonius' tactical arrangement of material). Poorly ordered arguments weaken persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery: voice, gesture, posture, and physical correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: His hands, his shoulders, the turn of his body, the stamp of his foot, his posture, his air, and, in short, his every motion, was adapted to his language and sentiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical delivery must match and reinforce verbal content — gestures timed to meaning, posture and movement that suit the sentence. Avoid mechanical or unrelated gesticulation (anti-pattern: beating time to the words).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enunciation and articulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Demosthenes was asked what was the first quality of a good Orator ... constantly replied, A good enunciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear articulation is foundational: consonants and vowels must be expressed so speech is intelligible and authoritative. This is presented as the foremost practical skill for orators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory and retentive recollection
rubrics_metrics.description: He had a quick and retentive memory...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong memory allows an orator to marshal facts, recall precedents, and deliver with confidence. It supports adaptability in debate and the ability to respond without apparent artifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and frankness of manner
rubrics_metrics.description: A frankness of manner which precluded any suspicion of artifice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An honest, open manner reduces perceptions of manipulation and increases audience trust. Affectation or obvious artifice undermines credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice quality and modulation (appropriate tonal use)
rubrics_metrics.description: His voice was strong and firm, though naturally hoarse;--a defect which he alone was capable of improving to his advantage; ... in capital causes, it had a mournful dignity of accent, which was exceedingly proper, both to win the assent of the judges, and excite their compassion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voice should be cultivated and used strategically: volume, tone, and timbre tailored to purpose (e.g., pathos vs deliberation). Even natural vocal defects can be turned into expressive strengths; misused voice is damaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized knowledge (legal/jurisprudential competence)
rubrics_metrics.description: He was the best Lawyer among the Orators ... could discover with the nicest precision what was agreeable to law and equity; and had likewise a conciseness and propriety of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When pleading legal matters, mastery of law, precedents, and equity is essential; legal learning bolsters argument and credibility. Example: Crassus and Q. Scaevola contrasted as lawyer vs civilian orator. Lacking subject-matter knowledge weakens authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry, study and practice (application)
rubrics_metrics.description: He applied himself very closely to his studies, and bestowed much of his time in writing and private declamation ... Notable industry and application were commended even when genius was lacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diligent study, practice, and preparation are necessary — industry can compensate for limited genius. Anti-pattern: relying solely on natural gifts without disciplined practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation of style to audience and occasion
rubrics_metrics.description: The style of the Stoics is too close, and contracted, to suit the ears of common people; so that of the [Academics] is too diffusive and luxuriant for the Forum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a style appropriate to the forum: avoid philosopher's precision in popular assemblies and avoid excessive diffuseness in forensic contests. Good orators borrow and balance qualities from different schools to suit purpose (example: Brutus borrowing Stoic reasoning and rhetorical training from rhetoricians).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of precedents, illustrations, and comparative examples
rubrics_metrics.description: He supported them by such a numerous series of precedents, that he overpowered Q. Scaevola ... he had an inexhaustible fund of arguments, and comparative illustrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing precedents and deploying illustrative comparisons strengthen legal and ethical arguments. Effective use helps overwhelm opposing positions when relevant and plentiful; absence of supporting examples weakens claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperament and manner suited to the role
rubrics_metrics.description: His style, as well as his temper, was too violent ... Rutilius was distinguished by his solemn and austere way of speaking ... some were rather rough and abusive, and much too warm and hasty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An orator's natural temperament must be compatible with public speaking: excessive violence or austerity can be inappropriate in certain venues. Temperament shapes reception; adjust manner to balance passion and decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art (technical skill) vs mere natural hits — reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Much depends upon Art: for though, even without this, it is possible, by the mere force of nature, to say many striking things; yet, as they will after all be nothing more than so many lucky hits, we shall not be able to repeat them at our pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetorical art — technique and learned methods — enables consistent performance and repeatable effectiveness. Reliance on sporadic natural inspiration is unstable; cultivate method and skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and truthful gesture over theatricality
rubrics_metrics.description: Reserve a share of [applause] for the quiet and unambitious performer who is distinguished by a simple truth of gesture, without any violence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understated, sincere gestures that truthfully express sentiment are preferable to exaggerated theatricality which can distract or seem insincere. Aim for authenticity in physical expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness, propriety and clarity in exposition (analytic skill)
rubrics_metrics.description: He could not only discover with the nicest precision what was agreeable to law and equity; but had likewise a conciseness and propriety of expression ... to explain what is obscure, by a clear interpretation; and first to discover what things are of a doubtful nature, then to distinguish them by their different degrees of probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear analytical skills — precise definitions, concise exposition, and orderly distinction of doubtful points — are crucial for legal and complex argumentation. Being prolix or imprecise undermines the ability to persuade on technical matters.
